items.question: How do you understand the problem that interpretability research is trying to solve in language models?
items.object: Interpretability research and language models' internal world models
items.answer: I think models really do contain reasoning steps that they do not say out loud. If you truly have a good language model, it should correctly predict the next word; to do that, it must internally have some kind of world model—of how people interact with one another, for example. We still do not know what that world model is. The goal of interpretability is to find out what that internal model actually is. We currently have no technique that is genuinely good at controlling a model's internal thoughts. If your model is doing something bad, nobody directly modifies its thoughts.

items.question: What makes interpretability research a natural direction for you?
items.object: Interpretability research
items.answer: I have always been especially interested in language. Then AI suddenly underwent such a huge change, and I tend to like thinking about questions scientifically, so I really wanted to study one question: what is the principle behind these things? But that is actually a very broad question, with many possible research directions.

items.question: What do you find most compelling about interpretability research into language models?
items.object: Interpretability research into the sudden rise of language models
items.answer: I think interpretability can indeed be approached from many angles. For me, the most compelling question is this: if we go back roughly five years, much of what we did in AI was not particularly successful, especially language models. People had used language models for a long time, but they were more for text editing, speech transcription, and things like that. Then something happened: suddenly language models became what everyone was studying, and people began investing billions in them. So interpretability research, for me, is trying to answer: what changed? Why did these things not work very well before, and why did they suddenly become so powerful now?

items.question: How do you understand Anthropic’s J-space paper as evidence of reasoning inside AI models?
items.object: Anthropic’s J-space paper
items.answer: I think it is a very interesting paper, and it adds another piece of evidence that models really do contain reasoning steps they do not say out loud. I have not read all of J-space's hundred-something pages, or however many there are, but I roughly understand the idea. The general idea is that we have something called the Jacobian, basically a derivative from calculus. We can apply it to a model to tell us, in the model's latent activation space—because everything is essentially vectors—which directions will cause the model to say certain particular words later. So, for example, ten tokens before the model actually says a particular word, if its internal hidden representation is moving in a certain direction, it may later say the word “spider,” something like that.

items.question: How do you assess the J-space paper’s contribution to understanding reasoning that language models do not express aloud?
items.object: The J-space paper and unspoken reasoning in language models
items.answer: One good thing about this paper is that it is actually a very elegant, very simple method, but for some reason it seems nobody had truly tried it in exactly this way before. Still, I think we already have a lot of evidence that these internal reasoning steps exist. For example, look at Anthropic’s earlier work on circuits. They have research called The Biology of Large Language Models. They showed that when a model performs three-digit addition, it can omit all the intermediate steps entirely, but if you look inside the model, you can find neurons that seem to record what the ones digit or tens digit should be. They have another example: if you ask a model to write a rhyming poem around a topic, as it reaches the end of one stanza, it is already planning which word should end the next stanza so that the next stanza can continue the rhyme. So I think, without question, models do things internally that they do not say out loud. And I think they actually have to if they are to learn language modeling well. You know, Ilya Sutskever is a very famous researcher in our field. He advanced autoregressive language modeling—modeling language by predicting the next word. He gave an example: suppose you are reading a detective novel, a murder mystery, and your task is to keep predicting the next word throughout the book. At the end there is usually a reveal of who the murderer is. You reach the phrase, “The murderer is.” To predict who comes next, you must in some sense model the entire novel, the entire story, and all the previous evidence pointing to different possibilities. So if you have a very good language model, it must be able to perform some kind of logical reasoning internally, right? Only then can it infer the correct next word in that example.

items.question: Why do you think analyzing a model’s chain of thought is worthwhile for understanding its alignment?
items.object: Analyzing a model's chain of thought for alignment and safety
items.answer: One thing I strongly believe is: do the simplest thing first. If I summarized everything I have learned from doing research, perhaps the most important lesson would be to do the simple things before doing complex ones. So inspecting a model's chain of thought is very simple, especially compared with solving interpretability, and therefore we should do it. In practice, when Anthropic, Meta, or OpenAI conduct safety audits, they do check whether suspicious content appears in a model's chain of thought, or whether the model is planning to do strange things. This seems able, to some extent, to help them find alignment deviations. So yes, I do think chain of thought is worth analyzing.

items.question: How do you think understanding the internal workings of AI could help society trust and regulate it?
items.object: AI interpretability as a basis for trust and regulation
items.answer: I think one application is trust. To trust a technology, it is important to know how it works. Think of regulators and government departments overseeing how airplanes are manufactured, how industrial machinery operates, or things like oil fracking. For powerful and potentially useful technologies like these, if we want to regulate them, we really need to understand their failure modes and work out how responsibility should be assigned when something goes wrong. I think regulating AI is very difficult now because, in some sense, we do not know how to prevent bad behavior. We do not even know why something bad happens, or who exactly to blame, because nobody truly knows where certain behaviors come from. We have enormous datasets and long training processes, so it is difficult to determine what causes a particular outcome. If we want to increase society's trust in this kind of technology, then even if we cannot achieve complete understanding, it would help to understand why certain behaviors occur. For example, if your doctor is using an AI system, both you and your doctor would probably want to know why it produced a particular result, right?

items.question: How do you view AI research's dependence on experimentation and researchers with exceptionally strong intuition?
items.object: AI research's reliance on experimentation and exceptional intuition
items.answer: Much AI research and progress has been highly dependent on experimentation. That is not a bad thing, of course. In our field, experiments are extraordinarily easy compared with chemistry, biology, or other things in the real world. So now it seems that many things improve because some remarkable people, or very smart people with very strong intuition, thought of certain methods. They do not know why the methods work, but they work. Google had a famous researcher named Noam Shazeer—I think he is no longer at Google—who proposed many architectural improvements that later enabled the modern Transformer, and he was also one of the authors of the original Transformer paper. He had a paper proposing Gated Linear Units, GLU, another architectural design. At the end, after showing all the experiments that these methods worked better, he said, “I don't know why these things work. I attribute it to divine providence.” It is pretty crazy to write that in a paper. It is as though he said, okay, perhaps God gave me an inspiration to try this experiment, and it succeeded. So I think it is a bit crazy that we have to rely on people with exceptionally strong intuition to advance the entire field. There should be a more systematic approach, or at least I believe there must be systematic reasons why some things succeed and others do not. So I think if we solve interpretability, we will be able to find out why some things work and others do not, and perhaps that can help us improve models more systematically or control undesirable behavior more systematically.

items.question: Why do you think interpretability matters for establishing trust in an AI system's alignment?
items.object: Interpretability as a way to establish trust in AI alignment
items.answer:
I think an important motivation for many people doing interpretability research is that we cannot completely trust what models themselves say, right? From the outside—from behavior we can observe—a model may appear entirely normal. Especially in a testing environment, it may perform so well that you think it can be deployed. But once you truly deploy it, crazy things may happen. Perhaps the model knows it is being evaluated, and once deployed it thinks, “Oh, now I can finally do what I really want to do.” Many people care about interpretability for alignment because we cannot always draw reliable conclusions solely from the behavior a model displays.

Suppose you have just met someone new. When you make a new friend, you want to make sure they are a good person, someone you can trust, especially before telling them your secrets or things like that. There is something interesting about people: of course we cannot always know what others are thinking, but society still functions. If you make a friend, something may happen—perhaps they make a choice in some situation that shows they do not actually have your interests at heart; or perhaps keeping your secret requires them to pay a cost, and they still choose to bear it to help you. Things like that are how we gradually build trust in others without knowing exactly what is in their minds. In suitable situations, a person's behavior somehow reveals their character.

I think alignment is somewhat similar. For these language models, or any AI system, one way to establish trust is to test their behavior in particular situations. Whether they make a particular decision can tell us whether their character is good or bad. Of course, you can get a lot of evidence from behavior, but models differ from people. These models run on computers. In principle, we can inspect every computational step involved in generating an output. And unlike people, we deploy millions of copies of one model. People pay for them to do all kinds of things, and we do not always know the intentions of the people using them. So this is very different from employing a human worker. With a human worker, you at least have a basic trust that even if they are bad, they probably cannot cause that much damage.

In this situation, interpretability research makes sense because the risks and consequences are completely different. And monitoring what occurs inside a language model is far easier than monitoring a person's mind. In principle, as long as we know what to look for, we can find it. We do not have to do anything especially crazy to determine “what exactly is the result of this matrix multiplication step,” right?

items.question: How do you think about what an autoencoder accomplishes?
items.object: Autoencoders and useful vector representations
items.answer: I would start with its basic idea: you have something—perhaps an image or a piece of text—and train a model first to turn this complex input into a simpler vector, a string of numbers, then reconstruct the original input from that vector. That is why it is called auto-encoding. The idea is that if you train a model to do this, then whatever strange input you give it, you can ultimately obtain a reasonably good vector representation. For example, if you can turn all images into vectors, similarity search becomes easier.

items.question: How do you think about sparse autoencoders as a tool for understanding and controlling a language model’s behavior?
items.object: Sparse autoencoders in language-model interpretability
items.answer: In interpretability research, the idea is to take all these hidden representations inside a model—perhaps vectors from layer 20 of a large language model—and train an autoencoder to turn them into a cleaner representation that is easier for us to study. Perhaps we can turn it into a string of numbers where each number represents something concrete and clear. For instance, if this text is English, this number is 1; otherwise it is 0. If the model is talking about rockets, this number is 1; otherwise it is 0. Something like that. A sparse autoencoder is a way to formulate this as a technical problem, so after feeding in the model's internal representations, we can obtain a relatively clean string of numbers. One nice thing is that if we get only numbers, perhaps some numbers represent the model displaying bad behavior or becoming misaligned, and we merely need to set that number to 0. But in practice the situation is messy. Things are not as clean as we would hope. The numbers themselves are not so clean.

items.question: How do you assess the approach of training a large model to make another model's internal representations interpretable?
items.object: Training large models with an interpretability objective
items.answer: I think this comes from a lesson from machine learning: if you choose the right objective and scale up a very large model around that objective, you get what you want. For language generation, that is next-token prediction. You only need to choose the right training objective to get a very good, useful model. So people are also looking for such an objective for interpretability, and sparse autoencoders are an attempt in that direction. The idea is to take a messy internal representation and aim to turn it into a clean string of numbers. There are sparsity losses and so on. But now it seems this may not be exactly the right objective, or it does not fully capture everything we care about. A recent iteration in this direction, also from Anthropic, is called a natural-language autoencoder. It is still an autoencoder, but rather than converting a messy string of numbers into a clean one, it directly turns it into natural language and then converts the natural language back, using extensive reinforcement-learning training to learn this. The advantage is that we are directly looking for something we can read. But the problem remains: how do you trust it? During training, the model began saying some rather strange things, and we are not sure whether that is because it has some internal language of its own or something. In any event, the whole idea behind this class of interpretability research is to train a very large model to solve the problem for us; we just need to choose the right problem.

items.question: What do you see as the advantage of Atticus Geiger's causal abstraction framework for understanding a model's internal reasoning?
items.object: Atticus Geiger's causal abstraction framework
items.answer: This direction comes from my research background in Chris Potts's Stanford lab. Atticus Geiger proposed a framework called causal abstraction. The idea is that if we have a hypothesis about a model's internal reasoning steps, we can test that hypothesis by intervening on the model. For example, if you think a particular direction in the model's vector space represents whether it is currently speaking English, then I can test that claim directly by adding or subtracting that vector, and see what happens. So we have a hypothesis-testing framework. Many people have had this idea: intervening on a model is a way to test hypotheses about it. Its advantage is that you can, in some sense, trust the experimental results as long as you chose the right hypothesis.

items.question: What do you see as the main limitation of testing hypotheses about an AI model by intervening on it?
items.object: Hypothesis testing through interventions in AI interpretability research
items.answer: I think a clear limitation is that we must study very narrowly scoped problems. Perhaps we can hypothesize how a model performs addition, or how it handles linguistic issues such as singular versus plural or subject-verb agreement. These are narrowly scoped questions. We can test them and find out many things—even precisely what a particular attention head or MLP does, and so on. But many questions we truly care about are not that simple. For example, if you want to know, “Is the model currently considering lying to the user?” it is not clear how to design such an experiment in this framework. So much current progress in this direction is trying to automate the step of humans proposing hypotheses. Perhaps we can give a language-model agent tools for intervening on a model; it basically does what a human would do, except we train a model to do it.

items.question: What do you value about the accessibility of interpretability research as its compute requirements grow?
items.object: The accessibility and growing compute requirements of interpretability research
items.answer: I think that is the problem. As the field continues to develop, interpretability research will require more and more compute. So I think one especially good thing about interpretability research so far is that even high-school students can enter the field and do research. I receive emails from Bay Area high-school students saying, “I ran this experiment with GPT-2 on my own laptop. I want to show you.” I think this may be one of the few directions in AI where you can still do that, because we have not really understood even very small models. But if a child wants to enter reinforcement learning, they have to buy compute first. Still, I think interpretability research is changing too.

items.question: What appealed to you about computational linguistics as a direction to pursue?
items.object: Computational linguistics
items.answer: Ever since I was young—probably since middle school—I have especially liked language. My family was multilingual; we spoke Hindi at home. Later I had some Chinese-speaking friends, and I became very curious about questions such as why Chinese differs so much from other languages. I was always fascinated by such questions. I later attended Georgetown University as an undergraduate, which has a very good linguistics department. At that time, computational linguistics was just beginning to become an important field. People trained LSTMs to generate articles or trained models on Shakespeare's text. There were many demos like that, combining linguistics, computer science, and the AI progress of that era. I thought that doing this direction could combine what I was truly interested in with work that might have practical social uses.

items.question: How do you understand the ideas that originally motivated computational linguistics?
items.object: Computational linguistics
items.answer: This field later changed a great deal. One idea at the time was that traditional linguistics studies what structures language contains, how language changes over time, and so on. Researching these entirely manually is difficult because there is simply too much data. So one idea in computational linguistics was that we still do linguistics, but use computers to do it. That was one strand. Another was closer to today's ChatGPT: people always wanted to create a program that could converse with you like a person and understand your instructions. But starting from scratch, that is an enormous problem with almost no obvious starting point. What do you do? One idea was that linguistics had already told us roughly how humans understand and produce language—for instance, how they process sounds and combine sounds into meaningful units, then combine those meaningful units into grammatical sentences. So the idea was simply to replicate the full set of linguistic structures we believed existed in the human brain, then write a computer program to perform the same steps one by one. Otherwise, how could you begin addressing such a huge problem?

items.question: How do you characterize the approach to computational linguistics research you used as an undergraduate?
items.object: Established computational linguistics research methods
items.answer: At the time I did not need to invent a new technique. Methods already existed. As an undergraduate, I mainly annotated data manually. I spent hundreds of hours doing that, then used the dataset I had annotated to train a model to predict those structures. items.question: How did your semantic-parsing experiment at Georgetown change your view of specialized computational-linguistics pipelines?
items.object: Model scaling and specialized computational-linguistics pipelines
items.answer: Something important happened for me. The Georgetown lab was working on a semantic-parsing task. My advisor was Nathan Schneider, and he assigned different students to different languages, though everyone solved the same task. Our model-training pipeline was very complicated: we would take a BERT model, add an LSTM on top, then a CRF. We trained such a complicated system, and it performed okay, around 60% to 70% accuracy. One day I wondered what would happen if I used a BERT directly—the largest BERT we could find at the time. Microsoft had released larger models. We only needed to fine-tune a linear projection layer at the end, without those complicated structures, simply train a larger model on the same task. It immediately achieved about 80% to 85% accuracy on the first experiment. I thought: so if I just use a bigger model, all those complicated things we had been doing are unnecessary. This was around 2022. At that time, so-called large models were still small enough to run on my own laptop, around several billion parameters. We could already see models continually getting larger. OpenAI released GPT-2 XL around that period, and Microsoft released larger DeBERTa models too. But the trend was already clear. Models kept getting larger, and all the tasks that we computational linguists thought were important would ultimately be solved automatically, without any special handling from us.

items.question: Why do you see progress in AI interpretability research as difficult to measure?
items.object: Measuring progress in AI interpretability research
items.answer: If I look at progress in other AI areas—for example, training a model to be good at translation, math problems, or Math Olympiad problems—we have corresponding benchmarks. You can have a model do IMO problems, for example, and if you want to check whether the field has progressed, you simply look at its score on that benchmark. But in interpretability research we lack a clear benchmark that can tell us whether we are progressing in the right direction, because progress here is genuinely hard to measure. Much interpretability work generates an explanation that is satisfying to people and is also truly explanatory, and both are hard to test.

items.question: How do you assess interpretability methods as a way to control a model's behavior?
items.object: Interpretability methods for steering model behavior
items.answer: We also made an evaluation benchmark for steering: whether your interpretability method can cleanly control a model's output without damaging its capabilities. We found that all these interpretability methods struggle greatly with steering. The best thing you can do is simply prompt the model directly or fine-tune it. The problem is that we currently have no technique genuinely good at controlling a model's internal thoughts. In practice, if a model is doing something bad, nobody directly changes its thoughts; people usually retrain it with better data.

items.question: How do you assess the robustness of using steering vectors to directly edit a model's thoughts and change its behavior?
items.object: Steering vectors as a way to directly edit a model's thoughts and change its behavior
items.answer: In practical applications, you may have seen Golden Gate Claude, which Anthropic deployed. That was a fairly fun demo. They used a steering vector to make the model keep thinking about the Golden Gate Bridge. I guess that if anyone is still using steering vectors in production, it is Anthropic, because they have said that when you ask Claude Fable certain questions about AI research or biological risk, they use classifiers or steering vectors to change the model's output. So they may indeed be doing something like this. Perhaps they have found a way to make steering vectors very robust. But in practical applications, based on what we in academia know and what we observe with steering-vector techniques, if you steer too strongly, the model performs worse at other things. For example, if you steer it toward the Golden Gate Bridge, it will of course keep talking about the bridge, but it may become especially bad at answering math questions. And this effect is unpredictable. If you merely fine-tune it to talk about the Golden Gate Bridge, it is actually easier to avoid these problems. I am rather skeptical that directly editing a model's thoughts is a sufficiently robust way to change behavior. And if this approach does not truly become popular in the future, interpretability researchers should look at what methods people actually use and try to make those methods better, or systematically explain why they work.

items.question: How do you understand AI research's reliance on case studies and edge cases?
items.object: The experimental, iterative nature of AI research
items.answer: I do not know. I think that may simply be characteristic of our field. So much depends on experiments. Long ago people might have thought: okay, as scientists, if we just find the correct, beautiful, perfect idea and apply it, we will ultimately get AGI, something like that. But in practice, the process looks highly iterative. People try a few things; models get better in some respects. Sometimes an idea really does have a huge impact, but no problem is ever completely solved in one go. AI research seems to work this way: you deploy a new model, collect feedback, and figure out what to fix next. So perhaps our whole field studies edge cases and keeps fixing those edge cases. Right?

items.question: What has interpretability research led you to believe about the mechanisms inside AI models?

items.question: Why do you see more value in explaining why a language model gets an answer right than why it gets one wrong?
items.object: Explaining why language models answer correctly versus incorrectly
items.answer: I think this returns to the edge-case issue. If a model gets something right, there is likely some internal mechanism that explains why it got it right. But if it gets something wrong, perhaps it simply did not learn the correct mechanism, or something very messy happened internally. There is a saying, apparently by Tolstoy, roughly: “All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way,” something like that, right? I think it is the same here. If a model gets something right, there is usually a systematic explanation behind it. But if it gets it wrong, perhaps—I do not know whether we can necessarily give a good explanation. So in some sense, determining why a model gets something right is more valuable than determining why it gets something wrong.

items.question: How do you see the potential of interpretability research to explain and fix model failures?
items.object: Interpretability research as a way to explain and fix model failures
items.answer:
Usually I feel that most errors are hard to explain. Even if we could explain them perfectly, we might only find that internally the errors are a mess, with no simple fix other than training longer, using a bigger model, or perhaps the model lacks enough capacity to store all the facts you want it to store. Something like that. But sometimes there really is a systematic explanation behind a model failure. I can give a more technical example.

Today's models basically all use the Transformer architecture. A major problem with Transformers is that their time complexity grows quadratically: as the sequence gets longer, the time needed to generate the next token also gets longer. People have been studying ways to speed this up. One research route is called state-space models. This is a bit technical, but I will try to keep it simple. State-space models existed in statistics long ago, but around 2019 through the early 2020s people began trying to apply them to language modeling, and worked hard to make them beat Transformers, because they are much faster. If you could scale them and have them perform as well as Transformers, you would naturally want to switch to state-space models. But people found they simply performed worse, even when trained on the same data, and did not know why.

Around 2021, a Stanford research group—students of Chris Ré—noticed a mechanism Anthropic had discovered through interpretability research, related to in-context learning in Transformers. In a Transformer, you give the model some prompts, it can understand and use that context to complete a task. For example, you want it to do a task but do not know how to explain it clearly, so you give it a few examples and it infers the rule for how to perform the task. Usually, the more examples you give it, the better it does. This was a striking discovery in the GPT-3 era. These researchers asked why state-space models could not do this. They had state-space models perform the same tasks, and they did poorly. Anthropic supplied an interpretability-based explanation: Transformers learn a particular attention-head mechanism which, when the model has at least two layers, lets it solve this kind of task. This is called an induction head.

The Stanford state-space-model researchers then asked what would happen if they put exactly the same mechanism into state-space models, to help them learn in-context learning. The paper is called Hungry Hungry Hippos—I do not know why it has that name—and its abbreviation is probably H3. They showed that with this change, or rather a simple but not quite small change, the model learned in-context learning. Many state-space models you may have heard of since then, such as Mamba or DeltaNet, have drawn on this advance. Now state-space models are fairly widely used. For example, recent Kimi or larger Qwen models use mixtures of Transformer attention mechanisms and architectures such as Gated DeltaNet.

So this is a very clear example where poor performance had a systematic reason, interpretability research helped us find that reason, and then fixed it. I hope there will be more examples like this. I think there may indeed be other similar things, and this discovery can be applied to other, larger models. If interpretability research makes very good progress, perhaps we can find more such cases.

items.question: How do you see the relationship between academia and industry in interpretability research?
items.object: Academia and industry as a shared interpretability research community
items.answer: I would not say I have especially much industry experience. My main experience was at Transluce; I have not worked at a large frontier-model lab, so what I have seen is essentially from the outside. My sense is that in interpretability, academia and industry share research results and progress to a greater degree than in other AI directions. I think this is because there is not yet a method where simply scaling it continually gives you better interpretability. For now, people still need to keep proposing new ideas, and ideas are something even a graduate student can contribute. Right? But in other fields, such as reinforcement-learning research, academia and industry conduct research very differently because the gap in the scale of resources they possess is too large. So I would say that in interpretability, academia and industry are still somewhat one research community. At workshops you see people from Anthropic, DeepMind, and OpenAI alongside Stanford, David Bau's group at Northwestern University, and Ellie Pavlick. Many professors do interpretability research, and their students do as well. I would not view academic research as useless; it is very important to moving interpretability forward. I think that is even true for industry.

items.question: How do you understand the dual-use implications of research aimed at making AI models interpretable?
items.object: The dual-use nature of interpretability research
items.answer: I think any genuinely useful technology is inherently dual-use. Nuclear energy, for example, can be very helpful from the perspective of renewable energy or energy supply, but the same scientific advances also brought nuclear weapons. AI research is the same. As we keep advancing coding agents, this can help all kinds of people who cannot program and have things they want to do in their lives but for whom no company has ever made a product or service. Now they can build those things themselves. But on the other hand, an ordinary person may suddenly gain frontier-level cybersecurity capabilities and hack into any system. So I think if something is truly useful, it will necessarily be dual-use. And as a society, we must also think through how to handle that. If interpretability research truly succeeds in discovering why models act in particular ways or how to improve models systematically, it will of course also be dual-use. It can help audit models, but it might also help a malicious actor discover how to make a model misaligned.

items.question: How do you assess the dual-use risks of interpretability research at its current stage?
items.object: The dual-use risks of interpretability research
items.answer: I think that is inherently unavoidable, but it does not mean we should not conduct this research. It means that, yes, we may need regulation or some democratic decision-making process to determine who can use such powerful technology. But so far, I would say interpretability research has not reached a point where it is dangerous enough in this respect. We have much work to do before it reaches the point where we truly need to worry about it. I gave an example earlier: interpretability advances drove improvements in state-space models. There may be a few similar examples, such as attention sinks, but such cases are not especially numerous. The reason is that interpretability research has not yet developed to the point where it can systematically produce results in this way. I am not particularly worried about this issue now. There are still a great many basic scientific questions to solve, so yes, it may still be fairly far away.

items.question: Where do you see the most exciting applications of model interpretability?
items.object: Scientific applications of model interpretability
items.answer: I think it is helpful to put these research advances into a real application. One application is that we can more deliberately design better models. Another fairly clear application setting should be areas such as drug discovery, medicine, and DNA models. Goodfire has a large life-sciences team trying to reverse-engineer various models used for scientific discovery, including DNA models. If we can figure out how language models work, that would of course be cool. For linguists, understanding how models process language would be very exciting. But the truly cool applications may be, for example, training a climate model to simulate climate, or training a model for protein folding. Can we extract from those models algorithms humans can understand and use those algorithms to advance science? Because we also want to know why they work, right? So I think its scientific applications could be enormous.

items.question: Do you think a more interpretable AI model is necessarily safer?
items.object: Model interpretability and safety
items.answer: I do not think so. If you know why it does something, you can also use that knowledge to exploit its behavior. For example, perhaps you can more easily figure out how to jailbreak it, or why a particular prompt did not successfully jailbreak it, and then find a more effective method.

items.question: Why do you see transparency about algorithms and AI systems as socially valuable?
items.object: Transparency about algorithms and AI systems
items.answer: Overall, I do think transparency is positive. From a social perspective, it is not especially good if we hand our lives over to complex algorithms we do not understand at all. People now have this discomfort with social media, because algorithms behind it keep recommending videos they like, which may consume much of their time and may be bad for children. If companies could tell us more transparently how these algorithms are trained and how they work, and why they recommend certain things, that could at least help us as a society decide whether we want them, or at least give us greater confidence that nobody is deliberately doing malicious things behind the scenes. Right? I think AI systems are similar. Many people do not trust AI companies or AI development and are very concerned about it, so having more transparency seems positive in itself.

items.question: How ready do you think interpretability research is to inform AI regulation?
items.object: Interpretability research as a basis for AI regulation
items.answer: I would say that ultimately enabling interpretability research to provide such tools is itself one goal of the field. I think that is part of why nonprofits like Transluce exist. There are many other organizations doing interpretability research that hope to provide regulators with tools to help them understand why models do certain things and thereby control those models better. The UK's AI Safety Institute also does interpretability research. But I would say we still have much to do. We cannot yet say with great confidence that we can directly use these research findings to formulate new laws.

items.question: How do you think interpretability could help control a language model’s personality during training?
items.object: Interpretability as a way to control language-model personality during training
items.answer: I think some interpretability research has already shown that the internal representations of different personality types seem to be organized in some way within the model’s representation space. Anthropic has a study on the assistant axis, which roughly says that helpful assistants lie along one direction, while if you get misaligned assistants, they are arranged in another direction. Interpretability has potential here. If we can use interpretability to guide the training process in some way, then it may become a more fine-grained way to control a model’s personality. And it may provide more guarantees than our current approach of relying solely on training data. Especially now that we do things like Constitutional AI, where, during character training, an AI decides what kind of reward a certain behavior should or should not receive. I think that is something we would want to be able to control, and interpretability may be able to play a role during training.
